text: White 12 took the ko first, and its capture threatens at once: approaching first fails, as White then takes four stones at C17. Black must retake with a threat, but White's group still has two liberties, so the retake threatens nothing yet. Black approaches, White retakes for free, and Black needs a second threat (Diagram 2). One approach with White taking first is S[A-1KO-], two threats more than White; with one, Black fails (Diagram 3).

Your S[A-1KO+] fits the sibling where Black's move 9 approaches at F19 and Black then takes the ko first (On the site, below); capturing at once with Black 9 costs that tempo. White's free move after Black 13 gains a threat on either side (Diagram 4). On that sibling and on the tree's other leaf ending with Black's capture at A19, your S[A-1KO+] leaves out the same gain, which raises the count there from one to three in the narrow area. So under your c121 rule the label is S[A-1KO-]; without it, S[A-1KO-3].

Both reviewers agree, and no open question decides it: in the counted form the fix would be S[KO-2], also two threats. The failure with one threat is decided in the narrow search area; in the wider one it rests on reading. The solver's bent-four test stayed undecided, but by reading no bent four can arise. The fix turns Black's move 9 wrong (On the site, below).

text: White 12 took the ko first, and its capture threatens at once. Approaching first fails: Black at B19 or C17 is self-atari, and White takes four stones. So Black must retake with a threat, but White's group still has two liberties, so the retake threatens nothing yet. Black approaches, White retakes for free, and Black needs a second threat (Diagram 2). That is S[A-1KO-], two threats more than White; with one, Black fails (Diagram 3).

White's local moves after Black 13 gain up to two threats (Diagram 4), so the full count lies between two and four. They work only before Black approaches, so by your c121 rule the gain belongs to the approach, and your S[A-1KO+] on the two leaves that end with Black's capture at A19 leaves it out too. In the counted form the fix would be S[KO-2], also two threats, but this tree writes approach kos in the A-form, and S[KO-2] would make the problem's result KO−2 and change 27 marks.

Both reviewers agree, and no open question decides it. The failure with one threat is decided in the narrow search area; in the wider one it rests on reading. The solver's bent-four test stayed undecided, but by reading no bent four can arise. This fix alone changes no mark. After the fixes Black 5 leads only to A-1KO−, against A-1KO+ after B17 at move 5, but stays correct: C19 at move 5 gives 10kKO, which besogo ranks equal to every A-1 ko.

Black's move 9 at a in Diagram 1 turns from correct to wrong, and the three moves after it in its line change with it. Its line ends in leaf k102, now S[A-1KO-], while b keeps its leaf's S[A-1KO+]. The problem's result stays S[10kKO], and the k103 fix changes no mark. A checker tried to show the new mark wrong and found it right.

After b, Black takes the ko first and needs one approach: one threat more than White (Diagram 2). After a, White takes the ko first, for free, and Black needs a threat just to reach b's leaf (Diagram 3), so a is exactly one threat worse. The solver agrees under both counts: with White's local moves barred, b needs one threat more than White and a two; with them, in the narrow area, b needs three and a at least four.

b's S[A-1KO+] is right, and the tree misses no better White answer to it. Not needed for the grading: c is as good as b, but the site rejects it as off-tree; adding its line lets the site accept it (Diagram 4).
